name: study_guide_v1
description: Twelve short passages from an invented study guide ('The Practice of Learning'), written for this evaluation so that the text can be shared and run through any model. They cover every knowledge category, dense and plain prose, several units in one passage, relationships, one complete, one incomplete and one image-only equation, a debunked claim, a passage that holds no knowledge, and a worked example. The facts in the text are the study guide's own; they illustrate the method and are not claims about the real literature.

review.prepared_by: AI assistant (GitHub Copilot) for the project owner, working only from the passage text; the extraction output was never consulted
review.notes: Reference results were written independently of any model output. They still need a human reviewer's sign-off before the status can become 'reviewed'. Names are the acceptable titles; each fact is a list of alternative words of which one must appear in the extracted unit.

passages.text: The spacing effect is the finding that information studied in several sessions spread over time is remembered longer than the same information studied in one block. A learner who reads a chapter three times on the same evening usually feels fluent, but recall a month later is poor. The same three readings spread over three weeks feel harder and produce slower progress, yet they produce much stronger long-term retention. Researchers explain the difference by the effort of retrieval: when a memory has partly faded, bringing it back to mind strengthens it more than re-reading something still fresh.

units.quote: information studied in several sessions spread over time is remembered longer than the same information studied in one block
when a memory has partly faded, bringing it back to mind strengthens it more than re-reading something still fresh

characteristics: relationship between an equation and a concept
passages.text: The forgetting curve describes how the chance of recalling a memory falls as time passes since it was last used. A common model treats retention as an exponential decay: R = e^(-t/S), where R is retention between 0 and 1, t is the time since the last review, and S is the stability of the memory. A larger S means the memory fades more slowly. Each successful review raises S, so the intervals between reviews can grow. The model is a simplification; real forgetting depends on the material and on the learner, and S has to be estimated from data.

units.quote: The forgetting curve describes how the chance of recalling a memory falls as time passes since it was last used
A larger S means the memory fades more slowly

passages.text: Memory is usually described in three stages. Encoding is the transformation of an experience into a form the brain can store; attention during encoding largely decides what is stored at all. Consolidation is the process, lasting hours to years, by which a fresh trace becomes stable; sleep plays an important part in it. Retrieval is the act of reconstructing a stored memory when it is needed. Retrieval is not a replay: each time a memory is retrieved it is rebuilt, and it can be altered or strengthened as it is stored again. Failures at any stage look the same to the learner, who simply cannot remember, but they need different remedies.

units.quote: Encoding is the transformation of an experience into a form the brain can store
Consolidation is the process, lasting hours to years, by which a fresh trace becomes stable
Retrieval is the act of reconstructing a stored memory when it is needed

names: Different remedies for failures at different stages

passages.text: The testing effect is the principle that taking a test on material improves later retention more than spending the same time studying it again. The benefit holds when the test requires the learner to produce the answer, such as a short written response, and it is smaller for recognition formats such as multiple choice. It depends on feedback: when learners do not find out the correct answer after a failed attempt, errors can persist. The effect should not be read as a reason to avoid studying. Testing works best after an initial study phase, because a learner cannot retrieve what was never learned.

units.quote: taking a test on material improves later retention more than spending the same time studying it again

passages.text: Retrieval practice can be organised as a short cycle. Before starting, gather the material and a way to check answers, such as a textbook or answer key. First, study the material once and close it. Second, write down everything you can remember, without looking. Third, compare your answer with the material and mark what was missing or wrong. Fourth, restudy only the missing parts. Finally, schedule the next cycle after a gap that grows with each success, for example one day, then three days, then a week. The method needs an answer key; without it, mistakes cannot be found. It takes more time per session than re-reading, which many learners find discouraging.

units.quote: write down everything you can remember, without looking

passages.text: The Study Loop is a framework that organises learning into three connected parts. The first part, Plan, sets the goal for the session and chooses the material. The second part, Practise, carries out retrieval and spaced review of that material. The third part, Reflect, compares results with the goal and adjusts the next plan. The parts feed each other: reflection changes the plan, and the plan decides what is practised. The Study Loop is meant for self-directed learners with several weeks available and is less suited to cramming for tomorrow's test.

units.quote: The Study Loop is a framework that organises learning into three connected parts

characteristics: evidence with numbers and stated limitations
passages.text: In a classroom study of 120 secondary-school students, two groups learned the same 40 vocabulary words. One group studied the words in a single 60-minute session; the other studied for three 20-minute sessions on separate days. Four weeks later the spaced group recalled an average of 31 words and the single-session group an average of 24. The authors note that the study took place in one school, used one language, and did not test whether the difference lasts beyond four weeks. Both groups reported similar interest in the task.

units.quote: the spaced group recalled an average of 31 words and the single-session group an average of 24

passages.text: Consider Maya, who has six weeks to prepare for a language exam. Rather than reading her vocabulary list every evening in the last week, she splits the 300 words into six groups of 50. Each week she tests herself on a new group and revisits the earlier groups briefly. By the third week she is cycling through three groups and notices that the first group needs only a quick check. On exam day she recalls the first groups better than she expected, which she attributes to the repeated spaced tests rather than to extra hours.

names: Language exam preparation with spaced tests
units.quote: she splits the 300 words into six groups of 50

passages.text: Chapter 3 begins with the cognitive basis of learning. Section 3.1 introduces the three stages of memory, section 3.2 covers spacing and testing, and section 3.3 describes a study routine. The chapter ends with exercises. Readers who already know the basic terms may skip to section 3.2. A glossary at the back of the book lists all technical terms.

characteristics: a claim the text rejects: extracting it as fact is an error
passages.text: A popular belief holds that each person has a learning style, such as visual or auditory, and that teaching should be matched to it. Controlled studies have not supported the claim: students taught in their preferred style did not learn more than students taught in another style. Learners do differ in what they already know, and prior knowledge strongly affects how well new material is learned. Teaching should therefore be matched to what the learner already knows, not to a supposed style.
